<reason>Both sides were disciplined, well-grounded, and format-compliant (proper Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure, no fake sourcing). A opened with a compelling asymmetry/chilling-effect case and cleverly turned B's own examples as "material-effect cases the standard already resolves." But B built a single coherent theory—ex ante enumerated lines versus an ex post general standard—and used it to answer every A thrust: the concession charge ("design, not gap"), the fuzzy-standards analogy (posture and scale: auditing motive from an employer's records versus auditing the world for proof of a negative), and the absorption of enumerated categories ("the general standard in a category's costume"). Decisively, B's Q1 forced A to defend the motion via "reasonable, good-faith business judgment," and B correctly identified this as an amendment: the motion's text protects conduct that objectively does not materially affect performance, so the reasonable-but-wrong employer is liable as written. A never reconciled this, and A's closing ignored the shapeshift charge entirely, while B's closing directly rebutted A's "speculative harms" and "no rival protection" framing. A's rhetoric was vivid and its harms concrete, but B left no live A route unanswered while A left B's central textual argument standing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q1 ("may the employer fire when the risk is clear but courtroom proof isn't?") extracted A's good-faith/reasonableness gloss, which B4.5–B4.6 and B5.2 converted into the debate-winning point: A was defending a reasonableness amendment stapled onto an objective-standard motion—"a rule that needs rewriting to be defended is a draft, not a standard"—and A never answered it.</best_rebuttal>
